newsitem.title: USA: Texas separatists free hostages as standoff cools.
newsitem.headline: Texas separatists free hostages as standoff cools.

text.p: Armed separatists demanding independence for Texas released two hostages early on Monday in return for one of their members being set free from jail, officials said.

The prisoner exchange took some of the heat out of a tense 12-hour standoff between the self-styled Republic of Texas and police, but officials said they had not yet decided whether to withdraw FBI agents from outside the separatist group's remote compound in the Davis Mountains of west Texas.
The crisis began early on Sunday when Bob Scheidt, the Republic's chief of security, was arrested by sheriff's deputies for carrying two assault rifles in his van when he left the group's compound.
Republic leaders retaliated by attacking the nearby home of a middle-aged couple, Joe and Margaret Rowe, and taking them hostage to use as bargaining chips.
They said the two would be released only when police set free Scheidt and another group member who was recently arrested in Austin on contempt of court charges.
After hours of negotiations, police agreed to release only Scheidt and the two-for-one prisoner exchange took place shortly after midnight.
But it did not signal an immediate end to the standoff.

"Law enforcement officials maintain their position and continue to discuss further action, if any. That decision probably will not be made until some time tomorrow (Monday)," said Laureen Chernow, a spokeswoman with the Texas Department of Public Safety.
She said Joe Rowe, who was wounded in the attack on his home, was sent to a hospital for treatment shortly after his release but added that his injuries were not life-threatening.

Rowe and his wife were targeted because they have been vocal opponents of the Republic of Texas group in a bitter local property dispute. Republic members said Rowe was "a spy for the de facto state government."

Republic leaders believe Texas was annexed illegally in 1845 and claim it should be recognised as an soveriegn nation with themselves as its leaders. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after it broke away from Mexico in 1836.
Richard McLaren, the group's leader and "ambassador," has been holed up in the remote compound since December, when an arrest warrant was issued against him on contempt of court charges.
It was not clear how many Republic members were inside McLaren's modest compound, which was once a volunteer firehouse.
The Republic of Texas first emerged in 1995, demanding the resignation of Gov. George W. Bush and other state leaders as well as the removal of all federal agencies from Texas.
McLaren was charged with contempt of court last December for failing to appear in a federal court in nearby Pecos on charges related to the liens.
